idea: How to prevent bad smells from drains
title: Why Unused Drains Smell (And How to Fix It)
description: Sewer gases enter living spaces primarily when the water seal inside a drain trap evaporates or is siphoned out. Standard fixtures utilize a U-shaped pipe fitting called a P-trap beneath the drain outlet. Standing water resting in this curved section creates a continuous physical barrier that blocks foul sewer gases from flowing back up into the room. When a sink, floor drain, or guest shower remains unused for extended periods, this trap water gradually evaporates, breaking the seal. Pouring water down dry drains routinely restores the protective barrier and stops bad smells immediately.

The image shows a realistic cross-section view of the curved U-bend fitting beneath a bathroom vanity drain pipe. Inside the U-bend, clean standing water is visibly filling the curve to form a proper liquid trap seal. The upper pipe connecting to the sink strainer and the horizontal drain branch leaving into the wall are clearly depicted with physically accurate geometry and threaded slip-nut connections. Neutral, clean bright lighting in a professional installation setting, centered composition with ample clean background space at the top and bottom. Photorealistic technical quality, clean piping surfaces, no text, no visual labels, no arrows, no logos, no watermarks, no fake brand names.
visual_story: The visual focuses on a cross-section cutaway of a standard P-trap beneath a drain outlet. Viewers can see how standing water rests naturally in the lowest curve of the pipe. This illustrates how liquid creates an airtight seal between the room above and the drainage system beyond the trap.

on_image_text.explanation: Standing water inside the P-trap blocks sewer gas from entering your living space.
on_image_text.takeaway: Run water down rarely used drains periodically to maintain the liquid trap seal.
